artworks.title: The Legend of Polydorus
artworks.description: Titian's Padua fresco cycle turns on Polydorus — Priam's youngest, murdered for Trojan gold by Polymestor in Thrace. Early Titian makes the boy's fate a civic moral for Padua: hospitality betrayed, a prince's corpse the spark of Hecuba's revenge.

artworks.title: Hecuba Discovering the Body of Her Son Polydorus
artworks.description: Meynier freezes the Euripidean and Ovidian recognition: Polydorus washed ashore after Polymestor's murder, Hecuba stretching toward her youngest. The corpse is the painting's centre — the Priamid whose death opens the queen's vengeance.

artworks.title: Hecuba Blinds Polymestor
artworks.description: Crespi paints the revenge for Polydorus: Hecuba and the Trojan women blind the Thracian king who killed the boy for gold. The Priamid's murder is the invisible hinge — Euripides' Hecuba staged as Baroque violence.

artworks.title: Hecuba Discovering the Body of Her Son Polydorus
artworks.description: Allar's relief returns to the shore recognition: Polydorus cast up on the sand, the youngest son of Priam as Ovid's ghost and Euripides' prologue. Nineteenth-century sculpture keeps the boy's corpse as Hecuba's turning point.

popCulture.title: Hecuba
popCulture.creator: Euripides
popCulture.description: Euripides opens with Polydorus' ghost: the boy Priam sent to Thrace with gold, murdered by Polymestor — the Priamid whose death drives the captive queen's revenge.

popCulture.title: Iliad
popCulture.creator: Homer
popCulture.description: Iliad 20 makes Polydorus the swift youngest son of Priam whom Achilles spears — Hector's grief at his brother's fall that precipitates the duel.
